name: Zerubbabel
bio: Zerubbabel led the first wave of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah under Cyrus's decree, together with Jeshua and other leaders (Ezra 1:11-2:2). His leadership in rebuilding the temple is told in detail in the chapters ahead. Once settled in their towns, Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, together with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his relatives, rebuilt the altar of the God of Israel despite their fear of the surrounding peoples, resuming burnt offerings and keeping the Feast of Tabernacles, though the temple's foundation was not yet laid. In the second year, they began the work in earnest, appointing Levites twenty and older to oversee it; when the foundation was finally laid, the priests and Levites praised the LORD with trumpets and cymbals as David had ordained, and the people shouted for joy — though many older priests, Levites, and family heads who remembered the first temple wept so loudly that their weeping and the people's shouting could not be told apart (Ezra 3:1-13). When the peoples of the land heard the temple was being rebuilt, they came to Zerubbabel and the family heads offering to help, claiming they too had worshipped Israel's God since the days of Esarhaddon of Assyria. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of Israel's family heads refused them, insisting they alone would build the LORD's house as Cyrus had commanded. The rebuffed peoples then discouraged and harassed the builders and hired counselors against them for years, eventually getting the work halted entirely through a letter to King Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:1-5, 24). Years later, encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo, Zerubbabel and Jeshua rose up and resumed building the temple, prompting Tatnai the governor to question their authority and refer the matter to King Darius (Ezra 5:1-17). The temple was finally completed in the sixth year of Darius and dedicated with great joy; the returned exiles kept the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, rejoicing that the LORD had turned the Persian king's heart to support the work (Ezra 6:15-22). Haggai later proclaimed him the LORD's chosen signet ring among the nations, a sign of special favor amid coming upheaval (Haggai 2:20-23).
